title: A million tiny crystals reveal how semiconductors form distinct cores and shells

content_html:
Perovskites and related materials called perovskitoids are promising semiconductor materials for solar cells, LEDs and light detectors. Their ingredients and internal crystal structures determine how they absorb and emit light. A chip just 2 centimeters across can hold roughly a million tiny crystals—becoming a miniature material library that can show how some mixtures separate into distinct cores and shells, changing the light they absorb.

Olivier Chevalier, Chad Mirkin and colleagues at Northwestern University have synthesized such a "megalibrary" chip of 1 million compositionally distinct, positionally encoded microcrystals in an effort to provide a platform to accelerate the discovery of optoelectronic-relevant materials. Their research, published in Advanced Materials, offers a map to connect a material's recipe to its atomic structure and optical behavior.

A laboratory in miniature

The team patterned a removable polymer coating on glass with a million microscopic wells, then sprayed different precursor solutions onto the chip's four corners. As the solutions overlapped, they created gradual changes in composition.

The recipes combined cesium with varying proportions of bismuth, antimony, bromine and iodine. Four chips covered a broad range of these mixtures.

Heating the templates produced crystals about 10 micrometers wide. Peeling away the polymer left an orderly array, with each position corresponding to a different mixture.

Crystals this size supplied enough material for both light-absorption measurements and X-ray diffraction, which reveals atomic arrangements. The team mapped hundreds of positions, with each measurement averaging signals from neighboring crystals.

The resulting maps linked structure to bandgap—the energy threshold for exciting electrons in a semiconductor. A smaller bandgap allows the material to absorb lower-energy light.

One crystal, two structures

In familiar lead-halide perovskites, replacing iodine with bromine generally increases the bandgap. Here, adding bromine could first increase it, then sharply reduce it, before it rose again.

Earlier work had observed unusual bandgap changes and signs that these mixtures separated. The new study shows how that separation is organized within individual crystals.

Chemical mapping and electron diffraction revealed cores enriched in bromine surrounded by shells enriched in iodine. In the core, atomic building blocks joined into layers; in the shell, they formed isolated pairs.

The layered core confines electrons less tightly, reducing the energy needed to excite them. That helps explain why it can have a smaller bandgap despite containing more bromine.

Growth observations supported a two-stage explanation: bromine-rich material crystallized quickly, forming the core, followed by slower growth of an iodine-rich shell. Calculations indicated that separation becomes more favorable as the antimony content rises.

The maps also exposed a practical trade-off. The composition with the lowest measured bandgap contained two structural phases. Other recipes offered a single phase. During a 10-day test in humid air, unprotected iodine-rich and antimony-rich regions degraded first, while bromine-rich regions remained stable. A protective polymer coating greatly reduced deterioration.

Mixing bismuth and antimony provides "a means to balance functionality and stability," the researchers write.

The study did not test a solar cell. It gives researchers a fuller basis for choosing candidates: a favorable absorption measurement can be dominated by one part of a crystal, concealing a second structure with different properties. It shows why changing ingredients alone is not enough—the atoms' arrangement can reverse an expected optical result.

Mirkin and co-author Chris Wolverton disclosed financial interests in Mattiq, a company that could benefit from the research. Northwestern also disclosed financial interests in related intellectual property.
